summary.text: Lenses and mirrors are everyday optical tools, and a common way to model light treats it as rays that travel in straight lines and bend when they pass through or reflect from surfaces.
The earliest known lenses were polished crystal from as early as 2000 BC, and the ancient Romans and Greeks made lenses by filling glass spheres with water.
In 984 the mathematician Ibn Sahl described a law of refraction and used it to compute optimum shapes for lenses and curved mirrors.

facts.label: Oldest known lenses
facts.value: Polished crystal from Crete, as early as 2000 BC

facts.label: Ibn Sahl, 984
facts.value: Computed the best shapes for lenses and curved mirrors

facts.value: Used glass-sphere magnifiers to show light reflects off objects

facts.label: Ray model
facts.value: Treats light as straight rays that bend at surfaces

items.prompt: A designer sketches how a magnifier bends light by drawing straight lines with arrows that change direction at the glass. Which model of light is she using?

options.label: A wave model that tracks diffraction and interference
A ray model that follows straight paths and their bends
A particle model that counts photons one by one
A full electromagnetic model solved for every point

items.explain: The simplified ray model treats light as lines that travel straight and bend at surfaces; wave effects like diffraction need a fuller model.

items.prompt: A medieval scholar argued that your eyes do not send out rays to see things. What did he propose instead?

options.label: Objects shed small copies of themselves that drift to the eye
Light leaves the eye and returns carrying the object's image
Rays leave the object only when someone is looking at it
Light bounces off every point of an object in straight lines into the eye

items.explain: Alhazen rejected the emission theory and proposed that light reflects in straight lines from all points of the object and enters the eye.

items.prompt: In the 13th century, Roger Bacon held parts of glass spheres over objects as magnifying glasses. What did he use them to show about the light we see?

options.label: That it streams out of the eye and lands on the objects
That it bounces off objects rather than being given off by them
That it comes from small copies of objects floating in the air
That it is made of tiny particles called photons

items.explain: Bacon used parts of glass spheres as magnifying glasses to demonstrate that light reflects from objects rather than being released from them.

items.prompt: A scholar in Baghdad wants to design a mirror or lens that focuses light as well as possible. What did Ibn Sahl show how to do?

options.label: Grind glass thinner until it stops bending light
Fill glass spheres with water to magnify text
Use a law of refraction to work out the best curved shapes
Place several flat mirrors in a row to gather light

items.explain: In his treatise on burning mirrors and lenses, Ibn Sahl described a law of refraction and used it to compute optimum shapes for lenses and curved mirrors.

items.prompt: Why is Euclid's treatise on optics seen as a turning point for the study of light?

options.label: It tied vision to geometry and so created geometrical optics
It proved that light is made of tiny particles
It described how to grind and polish eyeglass lenses
It showed that light behaves as an electromagnetic wave

items.explain: Euclid linked vision to geometry, creating geometrical optics, and considered reflections on flat and spherical mirrors.

items.prompt: Ancient Greek thinkers split over how vision works. One camp said objects cast off copies of themselves that the eye captures. What was the opposing idea?

options.label: Objects glow on their own, and the eye merely stores the glow
Light bends inside the lens of the eye to form the image
Copies of objects form in the air and are carried to the mind
Rays shoot out of the eyes and reach the things being seen

items.explain: The rival emission theory, first stated by Plato, held that visual perception happens through rays emitted by the eyes.
